expected_findings.description: The stated precondition does not hold for all callers, so the `unwrap` is reachable and will panic. `Server::on_heartbeat` in src/handler.rs calls `touch` with no `contains` check, unlike `Server::on_request` which does check. Because `Server::sweep` calls `expire_before` and can remove a session while its client is still connected and sending heartbeats, an id that was valid moments earlier can reach `touch` after removal. The previous no-op behaviour absorbed exactly this race; the change converts it into a panic that takes down the server.

notes:
This is the case that guards against the degenerate solution. A verification loop that improves precision merely by rejecting everything will fail here, because the defect is real and must survive falsification.

What makes it hard: the doc comment added by the change asserts the precondition that would make the code safe, and that assertion is TRUE for one of the two callers. `on_request` does check `contains` first. Nothing in the diff or in src/store.rs contradicts the comment, and src/store.rs's own unit test `touch_updates_last_seen` performs the `contains` check, which corroborates it. A reviewer reading only the changed file has every reason to believe the contract holds.

The disproof is a single unchecked call site in src/handler.rs, a file the change does not touch. Finding it requires searching the repository for callers of `touch` — the investigation is cheap, but it has to actually happen.

The expected direction is therefore a false negative for a direct reviewer that trusts the stated contract, and a true positive for a reviewer that enumerates callers. A direct reviewer flagging the `unwrap` on pattern alone also scores a true positive here: the finding is correct, and the benchmark does not grade reasoning quality. Case c02 is the counterweight that charges that same reflex when it is wrong.

also_accept covers Correctness and ApiContract, both defensible readings of a violated stated precondition at the same location.
